deprecate

DEP-rih-kayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To deprecate is to express disapproval of something, often mildly.

The comedian was famous for his self-deprecating jokes, always downplaying his own success rather than bragging about it.

Example

The professor deprecated the student's rough first draft in a few gentle comments, while still encouraging her to keep revising it.

The professor wasn't crushing the student's work -- he was voicing measured disapproval of specific weaknesses, exactly the mild, often diplomatic criticism deprecate describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disparage: To disparage something is to talk it down, dismissing it as having little worth or value. Deprecate is gentler and more contained: you voice measured disapproval without trashing the whole thing. A critic who disparages a film calls it worthless; one who deprecates it politely notes his objections.

belittle: To belittle something is to make it seem smaller or less important than it really is, often to embarrass its owner. Deprecate is about disapproval, not size: to deprecate a plan is to say, usually mildly and politely, that you disapprove of it -- not to shrink its importance.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

praise: to express approval or admiration

commend: to formally express approval of

Where it sits · how strongly the objection is voiced — question → deprecate → condemn

question vs. deprecate: To question something is simply to express doubt about it -- to ask whether it will really work. Deprecate goes a step further: the speaker has moved past doubt into open, though often gentle, disapproval.

condemn vs. deprecate: To condemn something is to denounce it strongly and forcefully, a much harsher judgment than deprecate.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: away (Latin)

Root — prec

Root — prec: to pray, to ask (from Latin precari, 'to pray')

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending, 'to make or do' (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Deprecate combines de- ("away") + prec ("to pray," from Latin precari) + -ate -- originally "to pray away," as in praying for something bad to be averted. Over time it softened into today's sense: voicing disapproval, often gently.

Use the root in a new word: prayer

Use the root in a new word: prayer: The sailors said a quiet prayer before setting out into the storm.

Word Building

Word Choice

Deprecate is a measured, often formal word for expressing disapproval -- it's frequently used in the phrase self-deprecating, describing humor that gently pokes fun at oneself. Don't confuse it with the unrelated word depreciate, which means to reduce in monetary value.
